channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [30] Comparative efficacy and acceptability of antidepressants in the long-term treatment of major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared the long-term (>12 weeks) efficacy (sustained response) and acceptability (all-cause discontinuation) of 21 antidepressants in adults with unipolar major depressive disorder using double-blind RCTs. The study aimed to inform treatment choices by synthesizing head-to-head and placebo-controlled trials.
FINDINGS: From 54,231 records, 115 studies (30,428 participants; mean age 45.3 years, 66% female) were included. In 35 head-to-head continuation/continuation-extension trials (n=9,888), escitalopram (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.21–2.18), duloxetine (OR 1.57, 1.08–2.26), and agomelatine (OR 1.40, 1.06–1.85) showed higher sustained response rates than fluoxetine. Escitalopram (OR 0.60, 0.43–0.83) and duloxetine (OR 0.64, 0.44–0.95) had lower all-cause discontinuation vs. fluoxetine. Bupropion and reboxetine showed lower sustained response, while reboxetine and milnacipran had higher discontinuation rates in pairwise comparisons. Sensitivity analyses including enrichment designs supported these findings, but 54% of trials had high risk of bias.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests modest differences between antidepressants in sustained response and acceptability, with escitalopram and duloxetine appearing favorable. However, high risk of bias in many trials and indirect comparisons limit certainty. The lack of patient involvement and missing demographic data further constrain generalizability. More high-quality, head-to-head RCTs are needed to confirm these findings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results may guide antidepressant selection for long-term maintenance, favoring escitalopram or duloxetine over fluoxetine in some cases. Clinicians should weigh modest effect sizes against individual patient profiles and monitor tolerability closely.

item.title: [21] Prevalence and outcomes of co-occurring mental/physical comorbidities and substance use disorders: An atlas umbrella review including 156 systematic reviews with meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesised 156 systematic reviews with meta-analyses to map the prevalence and outcomes of co-occurring substance use disorders (SUDs) with psychiatric and somatic conditions, aiming to inform screening and care strategies.
FINDINGS: High-credibility estimates showed ADHD with a pooled SUD prevalence of 21.0% (95% CI 17.0–25.0; k = 31) and major depressive disorder with 36.1% (95% CI 32.4–39.7; k = 161) among patients with opioid use disorder. Chronic opioid analgesic use reached 27.0% (95% CI 23.0–31.0; N > 3.9 M) in non-cancer pain and 40.0% (95% CI 32.0–49.0) after lumbar fusion. Hepatitis C prevalence was 61.0% (95% CI 56.0–67.0) among injection drug users. Syndromal schizotypy correlated strongly with cannabis use disorder (I² = 0%).
INTERPRETATION: The review’s strength lies in its broad scope and credibility grading, but overlap across reviews and reliance on observational data limit causal inference. The reported prevalences are clinically striking and support routine cross-domain screening, yet the review does not evaluate whether such screening improves outcomes. Effect sizes are large but observational, so implementation should proceed alongside trials assessing impact on patient-important endpoints.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider routine screening for SUDs across psychiatric and somatic domains, especially in high-prevalence groups such as chronic pain patients on opioids and people who inject drugs, while awaiting evidence that screening changes long-term outcomes.

item.title: [15] Mental Health and Behavioral Factors Associated With Suicidal Ideation Among Students in Africa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined which mental health and behavioral factors are associated with suicidal ideation among students in Africa, pooling data from 49 studies with 138,915 participants to inform prevention strategies in educational settings.
FINDINGS: Depression (OR 3.92, 95 % CI 2.05–7.49), hopelessness (OR 5.20, 95 % CI 1.99–13.60), and cannabis use (OR 1.44, 95 % CI 1.24–1.66) showed the strongest associations with suicidal ideation. Female sex carried a modestly elevated odds (OR 1.25, 95 % CI 1.18–1.33). All pooled estimates exhibited substantial heterogeneity (I² not reported in abstract).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is large but observational, so causality cannot be inferred. Substantial heterogeneity and reliance on self-report measures limit certainty. Effect sizes for substance use and internalizing symptoms are statistically significant yet modest to moderate; hopelessness shows the largest point estimate but with wide confidence intervals, suggesting imprecision. No funding source is stated in the abstract.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for depression, hopelessness, and substance use in African student populations may help identify those at elevated suicide risk. Clinicians should remain cautious about over-interpreting pooled associations until more longitudinal and interventional data are available.

item.title: [14] Dialogical therapy plus treatment as usual versus treatment as usual in adults with distressing and persistent auditory hallucinations in the UK (Talking with Voices-II): a randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The trial tested whether adding Talking with Voices (TwV), a dialogue-based therapy engaging directly with auditory hallucinations, to treatment-as-usual (TAU) improves personal recovery and other outcomes in adults with serious mental health problems and persistent, distressing voice hearing. It was a rater-blinded, parallel-arm RCT across four UK NHS sites (ISRCTN15897915).
FINDINGS: 309 adults were randomised (156 TwV+TAU, 153 TAU). At 8 months, personal recovery (primary outcome) was higher with TwV (adjusted difference 6.97 [95% CI 5.00–8.95]; p<0.0001; SES=0.63). Twelve of fifteen secondary outcomes favoured TwV (SES 0.18–0.86), including voice-related measures and PTSD symptoms; no effects were seen on dissociation or positive self-beliefs. At 14 months, recovery remained higher but smaller (adjusted difference 3.55 [0.96–6.14]; p=0.0073; SES=0.32). Serious adverse events were similar across groups and unrelated to therapy.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests TwV improves personal recovery and several symptom domains with moderate effect sizes at 8 months, attenuating by 14 months. Strengths include rater blinding, multisite design, and lived-experience co-leadership; limitations include reliance on unadjusted secondary analyses and lack of an active comparator. The clinical significance is plausible but should be weighed against implementation feasibility and durability of effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: TwV may be a useful adjunct for patients with persistent, distressing voices seeking personal recovery, but services should plan for sustained delivery and monitor long-term outcomes before widespread adoption.

item.title: [9] Is ibogaine treatment durable? 12-month follow-up of magnesium-ibogaine therapy (MISTIC) in special operations veterans with traumatic brain injuries.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This prospective cohort study assessed whether single-dose magnesium-ibogaine therapy produced durable (12-month) improvements in functional disability and psychiatric symptoms among 30 male U.S. Special Operations Veterans with chronic traumatic brain injury (TBI) sequelae including PTSD, depression, and anxiety.
FINDINGS: Of 30 treated participants, 25 completed 12-month follow-up. Linear mixed-effects models showed sustained reductions in disability and symptom measures (all p < 0.001 after multiple-comparison correction) with large effect sizes (Cohen’s d ≥ 2.18 at 12 months). Survival analyses in immediate remitters estimated 84 % sustained PTSD remission, 66 % for depression, and 61 % for anxiety at 12 months; however, most participants used additional psychedelics or other interventions during follow-up.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s naturalistic, single-arm design precludes causal inference; concurrent use of other treatments and lack of blinding/placebo control limit internal validity. The very large effect sizes are impressive but must be viewed cautiously given the small sample, absence of randomization, and potential confounding. External validity is restricted to male combat veterans with chronic TBI in a high-resource setting. Randomized, placebo-controlled trials are needed to isolate ibogaine’s true effect and durability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary findings suggest potential long-term benefit of ibogaine for TBI-related psychiatric comorbidity, but they do not yet justify changing practice; clinicians should await robust RCT evidence and remain alert to safety and interaction profiles.

item.title: [9] The gut microbiota dietary index reveals a modifiable diet-depression association varying by BMI and possibly linked to inflammation: a hypothesis-generating modified diet for future intervention research.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study (n=28,884 adults) examined whether a diet supportive of gut microbiota (Dietary Index for Gut Microbiota, DI-GM) is associated with depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), exploring potential BMI interactions and inflammatory mediation in a hypothesis-generating framework.
FINDINGS: Participants with depression had lower DI-GM scores than those without. Regression and generalized additive models showed an inverse association between DI-GM and PHQ-9, stronger at higher BMI. Feature importance analysis highlighted fiber, whole grains, refined grains, and fat intake. Exploratory mediation suggested inflammation may partially explain the association, though a high DI-GM diet lacks key depression-related nutrients (vitamin D, omega-3, zinc).
INTERPRETATION: The study is observational and cannot infer causality. The large sample size strengthens precision, but unmeasured confounders (e.g., lifestyle, medication) and cross-sectional design limit internal validity. The BMI interaction and inflammatory signal are intriguing but exploratory. The lack of clinically meaningful nutrient density in high DI-GM diets further complicates interpretation. Findings are preliminary and require prospective and interventional validation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support dietary modification based on DI-GM for depression management. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting these associations. Future research should test modified gut-microbiota diets with targeted nutrient supplementation in randomized trials before any practice change.

item.title: [6] Long-acting injectable antipsychotics linked to reduced short-term disruptive life event and death.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study examined whether long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAI) reduce all-cause mortality and disruptive life events (DLE) compared with oral antipsychotics in adults recently diagnosed with schizophrenia (SCZ) or bipolar I disorder (BPI). The study used data from Kaiser Permanente Southern California (2007–2019) and followed patients for one year after an initial mental health emergency or inpatient encounter.
FINDINGS: The cohort included 3,667 patients on oral antipsychotics only and 218 on LAIs. Adjusted analyses suggested lower risks in the LAI group for any DLE (risk difference −1.68%, 95% CI −3.44% to 0.08%, p < 0.10) and all-cause mortality (−0.46%, 95% CI −0.98% to 0.06%, p < 0.10). The rarity of outcomes and small LAI sample limited statistical power.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s retrospective design and small LAI group reduce confidence in the findings. While point estimates favor LAIs, wide confidence intervals crossing zero and p-values just above conventional thresholds mean the results are not statistically significant. Larger, prospective studies are needed to confirm any benefit on mortality or disruptive life events.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not yet justify changing practice to prioritize LAIs solely to reduce short-term mortality or disruptive life events. Shared decision-making should weigh LAI benefits against patient preferences and logistical factors.

item.title: [31] Psychological and psychosocial interventions for the treatment of antenatal maternal depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared non-pharmacological interventions for clinically diagnosed antenatal depression, addressing the clinical question of which psychosocial treatments are most effective and acceptable during pregnancy. Ten RCTs (n=1853) were included.
FINDINGS: Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) showed the largest reduction in depressive symptoms versus treatment-as-usual (TAU) with a standardised mean difference (SMD) of -0.83 (95% CI -1.38 to -0.28). Other interventions had smaller, less certain effects. Acceptability (dropout rates) did not differ meaningfully between interventions. The certainty of evidence across all comparisons was rated as very low.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (only 10 trials) and the certainty of evidence is very low, meaning conclusions are tentative. CBT appears promising, but the wide confidence interval and low certainty suggest results should be interpreted cautiously. The lack of difference in acceptability is reassuring. More high-quality, adequately powered RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and improve confidence in the evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support CBT as a reasonable first-line non-pharmacological option for antenatal depression, consistent with existing guidelines. However, due to very low certainty, clinicians should remain cautious and consider patient preferences and local availability when choosing interventions.

item.title: [15] Acute and long-term effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in major depressive episodes: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized sham-controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized sham-controlled trials examined how different repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) dosing parameters (total pulses, pulses/session, sessions, duration) affect acute and long-term outcomes in adults with major depressive episodes (MDE). The goal was to identify dose ranges where clinical benefits plateau.
FINDINGS: Across 108 trials (134 active arms; n = 5,621), significant non-linear associations were found between dosing dimensions and acute efficacy. The highest predicted acute benefits occurred at approximately 30,000–39,000 total pulses, 1,800–2,200 pulses/session, 14–16 sessions, and 2.7–3.1 weeks of treatment, with limited additional benefit beyond these ranges. Follow-up analyses (after >7 days) showed smaller, mostly linear associations, with optimal doses at 26,000–33,000 total pulses, 1,300–1,800 pulses/session, 10–14 sessions, and 2.8–3.3 weeks. Effect sizes were reported as standardized mean differences and risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals, though exact values were not provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides robust group-level evidence that rTMS efficacy plateaus within moderate dose ranges, suggesting diminishing returns with higher exposures. Strengths include a large sample size, rigorous dose-response modeling, and sensitivity analyses confirming stability. However, the findings are descriptive and do not establish individualized dosing rules. The follow-up data suggest maintenance strategies may be more critical than further dose escalation. Limitations include heterogeneity in trial protocols and reliance on aggregate data rather than patient-level factors.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results support using moderate rTMS dosing ranges (e.g., ~15 sessions with ~2,000 pulses/session) for acute MDE treatment, with potential adjustments for maintenance. Clinicians should avoid excessive dose escalation without clear benefit, but individualized tailoring remains uncertain pending further research.

item.title: [15] Trainee psychiatrists' views on clozapine prescribing in Ireland.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A cross-sectional online survey examined trainee psychiatrists' knowledge, confidence, and perceived barriers to clozapine prescribing in Ireland, a setting where clozapine remains underutilised despite its established efficacy for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS).
FINDINGS: Of ~500 trainees invited, 74 responded (14.8%). Most had clinical exposure to clozapine, but <30% reported specific training. Knowledge of clozapine’s indication in TRS was strong, but varied for therapeutic drug monitoring, dosing, and agranulocytosis risk. Confidence was highest in identifying TRS and monitoring mental state, but lower for physical health monitoring, managing adverse effects, discontinuation, and rechallenge. Barriers included adherence concerns, blood monitoring requirements, adverse effects, and delays related to hospital admission. Most trainees reported insufficient training.
INTERPRETATION: The low response rate (14.8%) and cross-sectional design limit generalisability and causal inference. Self-report bias may overestimate knowledge or understate barriers. While trainees recognise clozapine’s role in TRS, gaps in practical prescribing knowledge and confidence—especially in adverse effect management and monitoring—are evident. The findings suggest a need for structured education and supervised experience, but the study does not evaluate the impact of such interventions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current training may leave trainees underprepared for key aspects of clozapine prescribing. Institutions should consider targeted education and supervised practice to improve confidence and reduce underuse, particularly in areas like adverse effect management and physical health monitoring.

item.title: [14] Intimate partner violence and its association with mental disorders among women in the general population, pregnant women and postpartum women: systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the association between intimate partner violence (IPV) and mental disorders (depression, anxiety, eating disorders) across three populations: women in the general population, pregnant women, and postpartum women. The study synthesized evidence from cross-sectional, case-control, and cohort studies published between 1980 and 2024.
FINDINGS: The meta-analysis included 82 studies with 140,286 participants. For women in the general population, lifetime IPV was associated with depression (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.83–2.79). Past-year IPV was linked to depression (OR 2.36, 95% CI 1.61–3.45) and anxiety (OR 2.85, 95% CI 1.61–5.05). Among pregnant women, IPV during pregnancy was associated with depression (OR 3.59, 95% CI 2.48–5.20) and anxiety (OR 3.27, 95% CI 2.60–4.10). For postpartum women, lifetime IPV exposure was associated with depression (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.54–2.83). The certainty of evidence varied from moderate to very low.
INTERPRETATION: The findings suggest a consistent association between IPV and mental disorders across populations, with stronger associations observed during pregnancy. However, the certainty of evidence is limited by heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and exposure/outcome definitions. The predominance of cross-sectional studies limits causal inference. Confounding by socioeconomic factors or prior mental health conditions may influence the observed associations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for IPV in psychiatric settings, particularly among pregnant and postpartum women, may be warranted given the elevated risk of depression and anxiety. Clinicians should be aware of the strong associations but interpret findings cautiously due to the low to moderate certainty of evidence. Further high-quality longitudinal research is needed to clarify causality and inform targeted interventions.

item.title: [14] Ketamine for Co-occurring Chronic Pain and Depression: A Scoping Review fing the Dual-Outcome Evidence Gap and Its Treatment and Research Implications.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) examined whether ketamine, an NMDA-receptor antagonist with established antidepressant effects, also improves chronic pain when depressive symptoms are present. It synthesized longitudinal studies assessing both pain and depression outcomes after ketamine treatment, focusing on adults with co-occurring chronic pain and depression.
FINDINGS: Twelve studies (2007–2025) were included: eight with chronic pain populations (≥3 months) and four with primary depression (TRD, MDD, bipolar depression). Most reported concurrent improvements in pain and depressive symptoms. However, only two chronic pain studies used clinical depression diagnoses; others relied on symptom scales. Dosing regimens, study designs, and psychiatric comorbidity varied widely, limiting firm conclusions about ketamine’s dual-action efficacy.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous. The lack of standardized depression ascertainment in chronic pain cohorts and inconsistent pain phenotyping preclude causal inference about ketamine’s analgesic effects in depression. Prospective randomized trials with clinically defined co-occurring chronic pain and depression, standardized dosing, and validated outcome measures are urgently needed to determine efficacy and generalizability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data suggest possible dual benefit but are insufficient to guide routine use of ketamine for co-occurring chronic pain and depression. Clinicians should await high-quality trials before considering ketamine for this indication, and ensure careful monitoring if used off-label.

item.title: [14] Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in schizophrenia spectrum disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis of efficacy, safety and mental health outcomes.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve psychiatric symptoms, functioning, and safety in adults with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders who are overweight or obese and receiving antipsychotic treatment.
FINDINGS: Six trials (n = 446) were pooled, with only three (n = 102) contributing to the primary psychiatric outcome. Total symptom severity showed an imprecise effect (SMD −0.21, 95% CI −0.60 to 0.19; HKSJ −1.02 to 0.61). Secondary mental health outcomes (functioning, AUDIT, SQLS, BACS) were similarly imprecise, with all confidence intervals crossing the null. GLP-1 RAs significantly reduced body weight (MD −7.42 kg, 95% CI −11.52 to −3.33; I² = 94%), BMI (−2.77 kg/m²), waist circumference (−5.53 cm), and HbA1c (−0.36%). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent, but serious adverse events were not increased.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence for psychiatric symptom improvement is weak and inconclusive due to small sample sizes, imprecise estimates, and high heterogeneity. The cardiometabolic benefits are more robust but limited by heterogeneity and risk of bias. No conclusions can be drawn regarding cardiovascular outcomes, as these were not assessed. The findings suggest potential utility for weight management but do not support a clear psychiatric benefit.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GLP-1 RAs may be considered for managing antipsychotic-induced weight gain in schizophrenia, but their impact on psychiatric symptoms remains uncertain. Clinicians should monitor for gastrointestinal side effects and weigh cardiometabolic benefits against limited evidence for mental health improvement.

item.title: [12] Altered effective connectivity during cognitive distancing in cognitive behavioral therapy nonresponders with depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated whether pretreatment brain connectivity during cognitive distancing (a key CBT skill) could predict response to CBT in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD). It used fMRI and dynamic causal modeling in 77 outpatients before 25 sessions of CBT as part of the SPeED trial.
FINDINGS: Responders (n=39) showed greater modulation in a dorsomedial-to-ventrolateral prefrontal-to-superior frontal/pre-supplementary motor area network during distancing, while nonresponders had stronger amygdala-to-ventrolateral prefrontal connectivity. Nonresponders also showed decreased dorsolateral prefrontal self-inhibition during negative stimuli, suggesting heightened excitability. Distancing-related effects exceeded 99% posterior probability and predicted treatment response in cross-validation (r = .21–.31, p < .05).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides mechanistic insight into CBT nonresponse using robust neuroimaging methods, with strong internal validity due to dynamic causal modeling and cross-validation. However, the modest predictive correlation (r ~ .21–.31) suggests limited incremental clinical utility beyond standard baseline assessments. The sample was a well-characterized outpatient MDD group, but generalizability to routine care settings remains uncertain. Larger, prospective replication is needed before considering adjunctive treatment strategies.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support using fMRI connectivity during cognitive distancing to guide treatment selection in routine care. Findings may inform future multimodal prediction models or targeted neuromodulation adjuncts, but are not yet actionable at the bedside.

item.title: [12] Brief interpersonal therapy reduces anxiety during pregnancy: A randomized clinical trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether brief Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) reduces anxiety during pregnancy compared with Enhanced Usual Care (EUC) in a randomized clinical trial (CARE Project). Anxiety in pregnancy is common and linked to adverse outcomes, but evidence for effective treatments is limited. The population comprised 234 distressed pregnant individuals.
FINDINGS: Anxiety symptoms decreased over pregnancy in both groups (F(1,229)=54.87, P<.0001). The treatment-by-time interaction was not statistically significant overall (t(229)=1.84, P=.067), but IPT showed significantly lower anxiety than EUC starting at ~24 weeks (t(229)=2.14, P=.03, d=0.28). By end of pregnancy, anxiety was on average 5.2 points lower with IPT (t(229)=2.62, P=.009, d=0.35). GAD prevalence decreased in both groups (IPT: 46.4% to 13.2%; EUC: 47.4% to 16.9%), with no group difference in diagnostic status at study end.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest benefit of brief IPT over EUC for reducing anxiety symptoms during pregnancy, with small effect sizes (d=0.28–0.35). The lack of a significant overall interaction and no difference in GAD diagnostic status tempers confidence. The study is strengthened by its RCT design and adequate sample size, but generalizability may be limited by the inclusion of "distressed" pregnant individuals rather than those meeting full anxiety disorder criteria. Longer-term outcomes for mother and child remain unknown.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Brief IPT may offer a small additional benefit over usual care for anxiety symptoms in pregnancy, but the clinical significance of a 5-point difference on anxiety scales is uncertain. Clinicians may consider IPT as an adjunct, while awaiting replication and longer-term safety data.

item.title: [11] Effects of Group-Based CBT/ERP and ACT on Emotion Dysregulation, Sleep, Anxiety Sensitivity and Psychological Flexibility in Adults With OCD.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared group-based cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention (CBT/ERP) and acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) in adults with OCD, focusing on secondary outcomes such as emotion dysregulation, sleep, anxiety sensitivity, and psychological flexibility. This randomized controlled trial (RCT) aimed to assess whether ACT is non-inferior to CBT/ERP for these domains.
FINDINGS: Both CBT/ERP and ACT groups showed similar improvements across all four secondary outcomes (emotion regulation, sleep, anxiety sensitivity, and psychological flexibility) at post-treatment, 6-month, and 12-month follow-ups. The trial was powered for the primary outcome (symptom severity), not these secondary measures, so the findings are suggestive rather than definitive.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary due to the trial being underpowered for secondary outcomes. The lack of significant differences between ACT and CBT/ERP suggests potential equivalence, but this cannot be confirmed without adequate power. The study’s strengths include its RCT design and long follow-up, but the lack of blinding and reliance on self-report measures are limitations. More targeted research is needed to confirm these findings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ACT may be a viable alternative to CBT/ERP for OCD, particularly for patients struggling with emotion regulation or psychological flexibility, but current evidence is not strong enough to change first-line recommendations. Clinicians should remain cautious and monitor outcomes closely.

item.title: [9] Prolonged exposure, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing therapy, and cognitive restructuring versus waiting-list for individuals with PTSD and psychosis (RE.PROCESS): A multicenter, four-arm, assessor-masked, superiority randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter, assessor-masked RCT (RE.PROCESS) tested whether three trauma-focused therapies—prolonged exposure (PE), eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), and cognitive restructuring (CR)—are superior to a waiting-list control in reducing PTSD symptoms among adults with a lifetime schizophrenia-spectrum psychotic disorder and current PTSD (N = 162).
FINDINGS: Over 6 months, PE, EMDR, and CR each produced significantly greater reductions in clinician-rated PTSD severity (CAPS-5) than waiting-list. At 6 months, adjusted between-group differences were −9.76 (95 % CI −16.13 to −3.38; p = 0.0029; d = −0.90) for PE, −11.74 (95 % CI −18.04 to −5.44; p = 0.0003; d = −1.04) for EMDR, and −12.72 (95 % CI −18.89 to −6.55; p = 0.0001; d = −1.00) for CR. Secondary PTSD outcomes also improved; no significant changes were seen in psychotic symptom severity.
INTERPRETATION: The trial demonstrates large, statistically robust reductions in PTSD symptoms with PE, EMDR, or CR versus waiting-list in a diagnostically complex population. Strengths include assessor masking, intention-to-treat analysis, and clinically meaningful effect sizes. Limitations include the absence of an active psychotherapy comparator, modest sample size, and reliance on a waiting-list rather than an established treatment; replication in larger, longer trials is needed to confirm durability and assess safety in routine psychosis care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support offering trauma-focused therapies (PE, EMDR, or CR) to patients with comorbid PTSD and psychotic disorders, provided services are equipped to monitor for potential symptom exacerbation.

item.title: [8] Monoaminergic signatures of treatment-response heterogeneity in schizophrenia: a neuromelanin MRI study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) study investigated whether monoaminergic signal differences in the substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area (SN-VTA) and locus coeruleus (LC) distinguish treatment-response subgroups in schizophrenia (ultra-resistant, clozapine-responsive treatment-resistant, first-line responders) and healthy controls.
FINDINGS: SN-VTA contrast ratios were elevated in ultra-resistant schizophrenia (URS; d = 1.01) and first-line responders (FLR; d = 0.94) versus healthy controls. LC contrast ratios were higher in URS than FLR (d = 0.99) but not significantly different from healthy controls. Voxel-wise analyses localized SN-VTA effects to dorsal regions. NM-MRI signals did not correlate with symptom severity or cognition.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests distinct monoaminergic signatures across schizophrenia subgroups, with dopaminergic involvement in both antipsychotic-responsive and clozapine-nonresponsive cases, and additional noradrenergic involvement in ultra-resistance. However, as a small cross-sectional study (n = 78), it cannot establish causality or predictive utility. Effect sizes are moderate-to-large, but clinical applicability remains uncertain without longitudinal validation or treatment-outcome linkage.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: NM-MRI may eventually help stratify treatment-resistant schizophrenia biologically, but current evidence is preliminary; routine use is not yet justified.

item.title: [7] Testing the Impact of the #Chatsafe Intervention on Young People's Ability to Communicate Safely About Suicide on Social Media: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether the #chatsafe social-media intervention improves young people’s ability to communicate safely about suicide online. It was a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in 16–25-year-olds comparing #chatsafe with a sexual-health control condition over 8 weeks.
FINDINGS: 906 participants were randomized (453 per arm). Post-intervention, mean safety scores rose by 0.04 in the #chatsafe arm and fell by 0.23 in controls, yielding a non-significant mean difference of 0.27 (95 % CI 0.00–0.54, p = 0.051). Secondary outcomes showed significant gains in confidence and willingness to intervene in the #chatsafe group.
INTERPRETATION: The trial is well-powered and uses an active control, but the primary outcome narrowly misses statistical significance and the effect size is small. The secondary outcomes suggest improved self-efficacy rather than objective safety. Longer follow-up and real-world behavioral measures are needed to judge clinical impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: #chatsafe may modestly boost young people’s confidence in online suicide-related communication, but current evidence does not yet demonstrate a clear reduction in risk or change in practice.

item.title: [7] The missing piece: a case report of body integrity dysphoria with 5-month follow-up.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This case report addresses the rare condition of body integrity dysphoria (BID), where an individual experiences persistent distress due to a mismatch between their body identity and an intact limb. The report describes a single patient’s experience and 5-month follow-up after a medically indicated amputation, highlighting diagnostic and ethical challenges in managing BID.
FINDINGS: A nonbinary adult in their mid-30s, assigned male at birth, presented with severe limb dysphoria and self-inflicted tissue necrosis requiring amputation. Prior trials of sertraline, aripiprazole, and risperidone showed no improvement. After multidisciplinary review and ethics consultation, a right lower limb amputation was performed due to non-salvageable tissue damage. The patient reported immediate relief of dysphoria, and at 5-month follow-up, maintained resolution of distress, restored body congruence, and good functional adaptation without psychotropic medication.
INTERPRETATION: This is a single case report with no control group, making it impossible to draw generalizable conclusions about the effectiveness of amputation for BID. The patient’s distress resolved post-amputation, but this could be confounded by the medically necessary nature of the procedure (due to self-inflicted injury) rather than the BID itself. The short follow-up duration (5 months) limits conclusions about long-term outcomes. Ethical and diagnostic complexities are well-illustrated, but the evidence is preliminary and not sufficient to guide practice.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This case underscores the need for cautious, individualized, multidisciplinary assessment in BID but does not provide sufficient evidence to support amputation as a standard treatment. Further research is required before surgical interventions can be considered beyond exceptional circumstances. Clinicians should prioritize non-surgical management and ethical deliberation in such cases.

item.title: [15] Written exposure therapy as treatment for comorbid PTSD and SUD: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether Written Exposure Therapy (WET) is effective, feasible, and acceptable as part of integrated treatment for patients with co-occurring post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and substance use disorder (SUD). Twelve studies were synthesized, with six providing quantitative data on PTSD symptom change.
FINDINGS: A random-effects meta-analysis of six studies showed a large pre/post reduction in PTSD severity (Hedges' g = 1.18, 95% CI [0.68, 1.72], p < 0.001). Treatment retention was 69.03%, higher than typically reported for integrated prolonged exposure therapies. Most participants and providers rated WET as feasible and acceptable, though a minority found concurrent treatment for both disorders burdensome.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and limited by small samples, absence of comparator groups, and incomplete reporting of treatment components and SUD outcomes. The large effect size on PTSD symptoms should be interpreted cautiously given the lack of control conditions and potential publication bias. Retention rates suggest acceptability, but feasibility concerns remain for a subset of patients.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: WET may offer a brief, low-burden option within integrated PTSD–SUD care, but current evidence does not establish superiority over other treatments. Clinicians should consider WET as a potential component while monitoring both PTSD and SUD outcomes and patient burden.

item.title: [11] Antidepressant monitoring in secondary mental health services: a scoping review of current UK guidelines and recommendations.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines how UK guidelines address antidepressant monitoring in adults within secondary mental health services, using a scoping review design to map recommendations across suicide risk, adverse effects, physical health, and treatment efficacy.
FINDINGS: Out of 846 records, only one peer-reviewed study met inclusion criteria, while five UK guideline documents (NICE, SPS, RCPsych, Maudsley, NHS Trust) were identified. All sources addressed suicide risk and adverse effects, but only NICE and SPS provided specific monitoring recommendations (e.g., review at two weeks). No structured guidance was found for physical health monitoring, and recommendations for treatment efficacy were general and primary care-oriented.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak—only one peer-reviewed study and five guidelines were included, with significant gaps in monitoring recommendations for secondary care. The reliance on primary care-oriented guidance limits applicability to complex secondary care populations. The review highlights a lack of structured, evidence-based protocols for antidepressant monitoring in this setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware that current UK guidelines lack specificity for secondary mental health services, particularly regarding physical health and treatment efficacy monitoring. This may necessitate individualized monitoring plans until more tailored guidance is developed.

item.title: [8] Initial antipsychotic prescription and all-cause mortality after claims-recorded dementia diagnosis in schizophrenia: A nationwide propensity-matched cohort study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This nationwide propensity-matched cohort study (2002–2022) examined whether an antipsychotic prescription within 90 days of a claims-recorded dementia diagnosis in patients with schizophrenia was associated with all-cause mortality, and compared risks by antipsychotic generation and metabolic/QT-prolongation risk profiles.
FINDINGS: In 14,253 matched pairs (n=28,506), mortality did not differ significantly between those with vs. without an antipsychotic prescription in the first 90 days (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.976, 95% CI 0.939–1.015; p=0.2228). No difference emerged between first- vs. second-generation antipsychotics (aHR 1.018, 95% CI 0.946–1.095; p=0.6291). However, higher-metabolic-risk SGAs were associated with increased mortality vs. lower-risk SGAs (aHR 1.238, 95% CI 1.105–1.388; p=0.0002), as were higher-QT-risk SGAs (aHR 1.109, 95% CI 1.019–1.207; p=0.0164).
INTERPRETATION: The primary analysis shows no mortality signal from antipsychotic initiation within 90 days post-dementia diagnosis in schizophrenia. Strengths include large nationwide data and propensity matching; limitations include residual confounding, reliance on claims records (no dose/duration data), and inability to assess long-term outcomes. The secondary findings linking higher metabolic/QT risk to mortality are observational and should be interpreted cautiously; they do not establish causality or safety profiles for sustained use.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These data do not support avoiding antipsychotics in the early post-dementia period solely for mortality risk, but they underscore the need to weigh metabolic and QT risks when selecting SGAs in this vulnerable population.

item.title: [20] Effects of Tai Chi combined with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation on sleep and emotional outcomes in older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluated whether Tai Chi combined with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) improves sleep and emotional outcomes in older adults with sleep problems, a common and clinically significant issue.
FINDINGS: Three RCTs (n=211) were included. The combined intervention significantly reduced overall sleep severity versus control (standardized mean difference [SMD] −0.51; 95% CI −0.90 to −0.12; P=0.01; I²=43%). Results for specific sleep parameters and emotional outcomes (depression, anxiety, stress) were inconsistent and did not reach statistical significance.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and limited by the small number of trials, moderate heterogeneity, and lack of blinding in included studies. The observed SMD of −0.51 suggests a moderate effect on overall sleep severity, but the confidence interval is wide and crosses zero for some outcomes, indicating uncertainty. GRADE assessment likely downgrades certainty due to risk of bias and imprecision. No firm conclusions can be drawn about emotional outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of combined Tai Chi and rTMS for sleep or mood in older adults. Clinicians should await larger, well-controlled RCTs before considering this approach, and continue to rely on established first-line treatments for insomnia and mood disorders.

item.title: [19] Effects of opioid-free and opioid-sparing anesthesia on postoperative delirium: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether opioid-free or opioid-sparing anesthesia reduces postoperative delirium (POD) in adult surgical patients, a clinically important complication with significant morbidity and mortality. Forty-one randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 7,852 participants were included.
FINDINGS: Across the pooled RCTs, POD occurred in 488/4,013 patients receiving opioid-free/opioid-sparing interventions versus 633/3,839 controls. The overall risk ratio (RR) for POD was 0.641 (95% CI 0.525–0.784; I² = 52.2%). Subgroup analyses suggested benefit for dexmedetomidine (RR 0.612, 95% CI 0.471–0.796) and a nonsignificant trend for esketamine (RR 0.745, 95% CI 0.526–1.053), while ketamine showed no clear effect (RR 0.598, 95% CI 0.251–1.423). No significant publication bias was detected.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized and largely RCT-derived, supporting an internal validity advantage. However, moderate heterogeneity (I² = 52%) and some subgroup CIs crossing unity suggest caution in overinterpreting agent-specific effects. The pooled effect size (RR ≈ 0.64) implies a clinically meaningful reduction in POD, though absolute risk differences were not reported. Funding sources were not stated, and blinding details were limited in the abstract.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support consideration of dexmedetomidine- or esketamine-based opioid-sparing anesthesia in perioperative care to reduce POD, particularly in high-risk surgical populations. Clinicians should weigh potential benefits against known side effects (e.g., bradycardia with dexmedetomidine) and monitor for delirium using validated tools.

item.title: [16] Long term lithium exposure and chronic kidney disease in the elderly with bipolar disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational cohorts examining whether long-term lithium treatment increases the risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in adults aged ≥50 with bipolar disorder, and whether risk depends on serum lithium concentration or comparator therapy.
FINDINGS: Across six cohorts (n≈10 000), lithium exposure was associated with a higher CKD risk than non-lithium exposure (pooled HR 1.62, 95 % CI 1.25–2.11; I²=72 %, prediction interval 0.79–3.34). Risk increased with higher vs lower lithium concentrations (HR 2.07, 1.47–2.91; I²=42 %, prediction interval 1.21–3.55). Against valproate the association attenuated (HR 1.39, 0.77–2.51). Data on kidney failure were sparse and cognition was not reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is observational and at moderate-to-high risk of confounding; no study reached low risk of bias. The pooled hazard ratios indicate a modest, concentration-dependent increase in CKD risk, but the wide and sometimes overlapping prediction intervals and attenuation when valproate is the comparator suggest the absolute risk difference may be small. The clinical significance therefore hinges on careful lithium dosing to maintain lower serum concentrations and vigilant renal monitoring rather than blanket avoidance of lithium.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For older adults with bipolar disorder, lithium remains a viable long-term option provided serum levels are kept within the lower end of the therapeutic range and renal function is monitored against age-specific thresholds; switching to valproate solely to reduce CKD risk is not supported by these data.

item.title: [14] An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Synthesis of Service User's Experiences of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Psychosis (CBTp).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This qualitative meta-synthesis aimed to integrate service users' experiences of cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp) to identify therapeutic factors that may enhance outcomes. Twenty-four qualitative studies (n=334) were synthesized to inform future implementation and adaptation of CBTp globally.
FINDINGS: Three core themes emerged: (1) active collaboration fosters empowerment, (2) safety promotes trust, and (3) shared understanding aids acceptance or challenge of distressing experiences. The synthesis highlights that CBTp techniques are most effective when delivered collaboratively and sensitively, with safety and acceptance acting as prerequisites for therapeutic gains.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides a robust thematic synthesis of qualitative evidence, offering valuable insights into the mechanisms of CBTp from the service user perspective. Strengths include a pre-registered protocol, systematic search strategy, and independent quality assessment. However, as a meta-synthesis of qualitative studies, it cannot establish causal relationships or quantify effect sizes. The findings are limited by the heterogeneity of included studies and potential selection bias in qualitative research. The clinical implications remain suggestive rather than definitive.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review underscores the importance of collaborative, safe, and individualized CBTp delivery. Clinicians should prioritize therapeutic alliance and shared meaning-making, while cautioning against over-digitization that may undermine relational aspects. However, these insights should complement, not replace, evidence from quantitative trials on efficacy.

item.title: [11] Unmasking Panic Disorder in Adults with Leukemia: A Systematic Review of Prevalence, Risk Factors, and Management.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This PRISMA-guided systematic review (2015–July 2025) asked how common panic disorder and anxiety are in adults with leukemia, what risk factors exist, and how these conditions are managed. Seven heterogeneous studies (n = 1,292) were included.
FINDINGS: Pooled prevalence estimates ranged from 15 % to 39 % for anxiety and 2 % to 8 % for panic disorder. Younger age and chemotherapy were the most frequently reported risk factors. Two small studies suggested benefit from CBT and SSRIs, but no controlled trials were identified.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited to a handful of observational studies with variable diagnostic criteria and no randomised comparisons. Newcastle-Ottawa scores were not reported in the abstract, so internal validity is uncertain. The reported effect sizes are small and derived from uncontrolled designs, making it unclear whether treatment truly changes outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for panic disorder in leukemia patients may be justified on symptom burden alone, but high-quality trials are needed before recommending specific interventions.

item.title: [11] Prevalence of Self-Reported Self-Harm and Suicidal Ideation by Levels of Pain Intensity: An Analysis of the Australian National Survey of Mental Health and Wellbeing, 2020-2022.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional analysis of a nationally representative Australian survey examined whether self-reported pain intensity (none, mild, moderate, severe) is associated with past-year self-harm and suicidal ideation among 15,880 adults aged 16–85 years.
FINDINGS: Prevalence of self-harm rose from 0.9% (no pain) to 3.5% (severe pain), and suicidal ideation from 1.6% (no pain) to 8.7% (severe pain). The graded association persisted across sex and age subgroups.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s large, population-based sample and consistent dose–response pattern strengthen internal validity, though the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The absolute differences, while statistically detectable, remain modest in magnitude. Confounding by co-occurring mental disorders or socioeconomic factors cannot be excluded.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine brief screening for suicidal thoughts in patients reporting moderate or severe pain may be justified, but the small absolute risks do not mandate universal risk assessment in all pain presentations.

item.title: [9] Prescription Patterns in Canadian Operational Stress Injury Clinics: An In-Depth Examination of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Treatment Practices.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This nationwide survey examined pharmacotherapy prescribing patterns for PTSD in Canadian operational stress injury (OSI) clinics, focusing on alignment with guideline recommendations and the influence of patient complexity. The study used a two-part survey of psychiatrists and collected patient-level data to assess real-world treatment practices in a specialized military/veteran PTSD care setting.
FINDINGS: Twenty psychiatrists provided data on 438 patients with long-standing PTSD (mean duration 8.2 years), high comorbidity, and extensive prior pharmacotherapy. Nearly all patients (98.6%) were prescribed at least one PTSD-related medication, with an average of three per patient. SSRIs/SNRIs were commonly used as first-line agents, but adjunctive hypnotics, antiadrenergic agents, antipsychotics, and benzodiazepines were frequently added, reflecting polypharmacy. Substantial intersite variability in prescribing was observed.
INTERPRETATION: The study highlights real-world challenges in treating complex, chronic PTSD despite adherence to guideline-recommended first-line agents. The high rate of polypharmacy and variability across sites suggest uncertainty in optimal sequencing or combination strategies. The descriptive design and lack of clinical outcome data limit causal inference, and the sample may not represent general psychiatric populations. The findings are preliminary and underscore the need for pragmatic trials to guide stepped-care approaches in complex PTSD.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware of frequent polypharmacy and intersite variability in PTSD treatment within specialized clinics. Current evidence does not support specific adjunctive strategies, so individualized, symptom-targeted prescribing remains necessary, with caution regarding benzodiazepines and antipsychotics due to limited long-term benefit and potential harms.

item.title: [9] THE EFFECTIVENESS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL INTERVENTIONS IN MANAGING ANXIETY AND STRESS FOLLOWING TRAUMATIC EVENTS.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (TF-CBT) or mindfulness-based approaches reduce anxiety, stress and PTSD symptoms after traumatic events, using a three-arm controlled design with 240 adults and 8-week follow-up.
FINDINGS: Both TF-CBT and mindfulness groups showed statistically significant improvements versus control on GAD-7, PSS-10 and PCL-5 at post-treatment (p≤0.01), which persisted at 8 weeks. Regression indicated therapy duration (β=-0.62, p<0.001) and baseline severity (β=0.49, p=0.01) explained 55% of outcome variance; TF-CBT outperformed mindfulness.
INTERPRETATION: The randomized allocation and use of validated scales strengthen internal validity, but the absence of assessor blinding, reliance on self-report measures, and modest sample size raise risk of bias. The 8-week follow-up is short for long-term claims. Effect sizes are not reported, so clinical significance remains uncertain despite statistical significance.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: TF-CBT may be prioritized over mindfulness for post-traumatic symptoms, but clinicians should await longer follow-up and larger, blinded trials before changing first-line recommendations.

item.title: [7] Phytocannabinoids in neurologic, neuropsychiatric, inflammatory, pain, cardiometabolic, hepatic, renal, and neoplastic disorders: Pharmacology, clinical evidence, and translational perspectives.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a narrative review examining the pharmacology, safety, and therapeutic evidence for phytocannabinoids (e.g., THC, CBD) across multiple medical disorders, including neurologic, neuropsychiatric, and pain conditions. It synthesizes molecular mechanisms, clinical efficacy, and translational perspectives to guide future research and clinical use.
FINDINGS: The strongest clinical evidence supports pharmaceutical-grade oral CBD as adjunctive therapy for seizures in Dravet syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis complex, and standardized THC-CBD formulations for spasticity in multiple sclerosis. Emerging signals exist for schizophrenia, pain, fibromyalgia, sleep disturbance, and substance-use disorders, but efficacy is compound-, formulation-, and indication-specific. Preclinical data suggest potential benefits in neurodegeneration, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and immune-mediated disorders, though translation is limited by product heterogeneity and underpowered trials.
INTERPRETATION: This review provides a broad overview but lacks quantitative synthesis (e.g., effect sizes, confidence intervals) due to its narrative nature. Strengths include comprehensive coverage of mechanisms and indications, but weaknesses include reliance on preclinical data and low-certainty clinical signals. The evidence base is strongest for epilepsy and MS spasticity, while other indications remain preliminary. High heterogeneity in formulations and dosing complicates interpretation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current clinical use should be restricted to approved indications (e.g., CBD for epilepsy, THC-CBD for MS spasticity). For other conditions, evidence is insufficient to recommend routine use; clinicians should await higher-quality trials before considering cannabinoids as standard therapy.

item.title: [6] Comorbidity of chronic musculoskeletal pain, depression, anxiety and sleep problems.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the comorbidity of chronic musculoskeletal pain (CMP) with depression, anxiety, and sleep problems, highlighting the clinical and mechanistic overlap and summarizing recent evidence on prevalence and management.
FINDINGS: Approximately 40% of individuals with chronic pain meet criteria for clinically significant depression and/or anxiety, while up to 75% report sleep problems. Comorbid psychiatric symptoms are linked to greater functional impairment and reduced quality of life. Psychotherapies such as cognitive behavioral therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy show benefit, and duloxetine demonstrates efficacy across pain, mood, anxiety, sleep, and quality-of-life domains in CMP.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper synthesizes existing literature without formal quality appraisal or quantitative synthesis, so conclusions rely on the cited studies’ internal validity. The high prevalence estimates and mechanistic explanations are consistent with prior research, but effect sizes and comparator details are not reported here. The clinical recommendations are plausible but not directly supported by effect estimates in this summary.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should screen for depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbance in patients with CMP and consider integrating mental health specialists into multidisciplinary care teams. Duloxetine may be considered when mood, anxiety, and sleep symptoms co-occur, but treatment choices should be individualized based on patient preference and side-effect profiles.

item.title: [6] Abnormal inferior parietal hub configuration during mindfulness following rumination in remitted depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional fMRI study examined how brain network hubs reconfigure when patients with remitted depression (RD) shift from rumination to mindfulness, compared with healthy controls (HCs). It asked whether RD shows abnormal inferior parietal lobule (IPL) hub function during mindfulness, a potential mechanism for relapse risk.
FINDINGS: Fifty-one RD patients and 41 HCs underwent a six-state fMRI paradigm. During mindfulness, RD showed a hyperconnected network component linking default mode, attention, and frontoparietal networks, anchored in a left IPL hub. Graph-theoretical analyses revealed reduced degree centrality, betweenness centrality, and nodal efficiency in the left IPL in RD (all FDR-corrected p < 0.05). The similarity of IPL connectivity profiles from rumination to mindfulness was significantly lower in RD versus HCs. Within RD, IPL metrics correlated negatively with rumination severity (RRS).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence that RD is associated with inefficient IPL hub reconfiguration during mindfulness following rumination, suggesting a residual vulnerability. Strengths include the multi-state fMRI design and use of graph-theoretical metrics. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the clinical significance of small-to-moderate network changes remains uncertain. The exploratory nature and lack of clinical outcome data limit generalisability to routine care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings suggest that inefficient IPL hub reconfiguration during mindfulness may be a candidate biomarker for residual vulnerability in RD, potentially guiding monitoring or targeted interventions, but current evidence is too preliminary to change practice.

item.title: [6] Comparative Risk of Suicide-Related Events Across Antidepressant Classes in Autistic Individuals: A New-User Active Comparator Cohort Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study addressed whether different classes of antidepressants are associated with varying risks of suicide-related events (SREs) in autistic individuals, a population with limited comparative safety data. Using a retrospective new-user active-comparator cohort design, researchers analyzed electronic health records from 42,441 autistic individuals initiating antidepressants, comparing SSRIs, atypical antidepressants, SNRIs, and TCAs.
FINDINGS: In a cohort of 42,441 autistic antidepressant initiators, atypical antidepressants showed a lower hazard of SREs compared to SSRIs (HR 0.787, 95% CI 0.632–0.979), and TCAs showed an even lower hazard (HR 0.487, 95% CI 0.263–0.902). No clear difference was observed for SNRIs versus SSRIs (HR 0.948, 95% CI 0.651–1.381). Among individual agents, trazodone was associated with lower SRE risk than SSRIs, while bupropion and mirtazapine showed no clear difference. Exploratory analyses suggested a potential age-related effect, with lower hazards for atypicals versus SSRIs in those under 18, though this was inconsistent.
INTERPRETATION: The study benefits from a large, real-world sample and robust statistical methods (propensity score overlap weighting, Cox models), enhancing internal validity. However, as an observational cohort, residual confounding by indication and unmeasured variables (e.g., severity of depression, clinician decision-making) remains a concern. The effect sizes are modest and not uniform across drug classes or agents, and findings for age subgroups are exploratory. The study does not establish causality, and the confidence intervals for some comparisons are wide, limiting precision.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest potential differences in suicide-related safety among antidepressants in autistic individuals, particularly favoring atypicals and TCAs over SSRIs. However, given the observational design and modest effect sizes, these results should not drive immediate changes in prescribing without further confirmatory research. Clinicians should continue to monitor closely for suicide-related outcomes regardless of antidepressant class, especially in autistic youth.

item.title: [23] Cost-Effectiveness of Early Dose Reduction or Discontinuation Versus Antipsychotic Maintenance After First-Episode Psychosis: Results From the HAMLETT Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study assessed the cost-effectiveness of early antipsychotic dose reduction or discontinuation versus maintenance treatment in 347 remitted first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients over 24 months, using a trial-based cost-utility analysis alongside the HAMLETT RCT. The clinical question was whether reducing or stopping antipsychotics after remission is a cost-effective alternative to standard maintenance therapy.
FINDINGS: Early dose reduction/discontinuation led to lower QALYs (-0.077) and higher costs (€23,563) compared to maintenance over 24 months. The incremental net monetary benefit was -€27,430 at a €50,000/QALY threshold, with only ~9% probability of being cost-effective. A subgroup analysis suggested a small, uncertain benefit among female participants.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is robust due to the RCT design, societal perspective, and sensitivity analyses, but the 24-month horizon may be too short to capture long-term benefits (e.g., metabolic or functional gains). The negative cost-effectiveness result is consistent across scenarios, though subgroup findings warrant cautious exploration. The study’s funding sources are not reported, which is a minor limitation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, maintenance antipsychotic treatment after FEP remission remains the more cost-effective strategy. Clinicians should individualize decisions, particularly for female patients, but prioritize evidence-based maintenance unless clear benefits of reduction emerge over longer follow-up.

item.title: [17] HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY IN ALCOHOL-RELATED CIRRHOSIS:A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS, THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES, AND PROGNOSTIC OUTCOMES.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA 2020) examined hepatic encephalopathy (HE) in alcohol-related cirrhosis (ARC), synthesizing evidence from 14 studies (n=6,185) to clarify clinical characteristics, treatments, and outcomes in this understudied subgroup.
FINDINGS: HE prevalence in ARC was 18.5% during hospitalization, with 90-day mortality at 12.1%. HE correlated with higher mortality (HR 3.1 at 90 days; HR 2.9 at 1 year), and active alcohol use worsened prognosis (HR 2.5). For secondary prophylaxis, rifaximin reduced recurrence (HR 0.42), often as adjunct to lactulose; lactulose alone also outperformed placebo. In acute HE, polyethylene glycol showed faster improvement than lactulose, though evidence was sparse.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is low-certainty (GRADE) due to heterogeneity, mixed-etiology cohorts, and observational designs with potential confounding. While associations between HE, mortality, and alcohol use are strong, causality cannot be inferred. The rifaximin and lactulose data are suggestive but rely on small, indirect studies. Polyethylene glycol’s benefit is preliminary and warrants further RCT validation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support aggressive secondary prophylaxis (rifaximin + lactulose) in ARC-related HE, but definitive ARC-specific guidelines are lacking. Clinicians should prioritize alcohol abstinence and monitor HE recurrence closely; polyethylene glycol may be considered for acute HE pending stronger trials.

item.title: [15] Ketamine/Esketamine in Clinical Practice: Areas of Consensus and Nonconsensus from an American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) Delphi Panel Task Force.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) Delphi panel sought expert consensus on practical use of ketamine/esketamine for mood disorders in real-world settings, where evidence lags behind clinical implementation. The task force comprised 21 international academic psychiatrists with ketamine/esketamine expertise.
FINDINGS: Consensus (≥75% agreement) was reached on 35 of 105 items (33%), covering diagnostic indications, contraindications, dosing limits, racemic vs enantiomeric preparations, delivery routes, safety monitoring, access, and outcome criteria. Major areas of non-consensus included novel formulations (oral/IM), high-dose infusions, ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and use beyond major depressive disorder.
INTERPRETATION: The low consensus rate (33%) highlights substantial uncertainty and gaps between real-world practice and the evidence base. Strengths include a structured Delphi process with predefined consensus thresholds and expert input; limitations include reliance on expert opinion rather than empirical data and potential selection bias among panel members. The findings underscore the need for targeted research to inform routine care decisions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice lacks robust evidence for many key decisions; clinicians should proceed cautiously, prioritize safety monitoring, and consider enrolling patients in studies to address uncertainties, especially regarding novel formulations and indications.

item.title: [15] Internet-based exercise interventions for the treatment of depression and anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) examined whether internet-based structured exercise interventions reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety compared with non-exercise controls in adults, addressing access barriers to conventional treatments.
FINDINGS: Across 11 RCTs (n=1,066), internet-based exercise produced a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms (standardised mean difference [SMD] −0.53, 95% CI −0.80 to −0.26; I²=77.2%). In 7 RCTs (n=607), a smaller but statistically significant reduction in anxiety symptoms was observed (SMD −0.41, 95% CI −0.65 to −0.17; I²=48.9%). Most trials had “some concerns” for risk of bias, and the certainty of evidence was rated low for depression and moderate for anxiety.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests internet-based exercise can modestly alleviate depressive and anxiety symptoms, but high heterogeneity for depression and risk-of-bias concerns limit confidence. The moderate-certainty finding for anxiety is more robust, yet effect sizes are small-to-moderate and may not translate to clinically meaningful changes for all patients. Long-term durability and implementation in routine care remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Internet-based exercise could serve as an adjunctive, low-risk option for patients unable or unwilling to engage in face-to-face therapy, but clinicians should set expectations about modest benefits and monitor symptom trajectories closely.

item.title: [14] Establishing the Clinical Role of Digital Therapeutics in Major Depressive Disorder Treatment: A Consensus Panel Perspective.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A multidisciplinary expert consensus panel (May 2026) addressed how digital therapeutics (DTx) for major depressive disorder (MDD) should be evaluated, selected, and implemented in routine care across the US and Europe, given growing evidence of efficacy but low clinical adoption.
FINDINGS: The panel issued four consensus statements: DTx are a distinct treatment category to be judged primarily on efficacy; they can be used at multiple stepped-care stages (e.g., bridge-to-care, augmentation); clinician unfamiliarity, implementation hurdles, and engagement uncertainty are key barriers; and recommendations aim to guide clinician selection and integration of evidence-based DTx.
INTERPRETATION: This is a consensus document, not empirical research, so its strength lies in expert agreement rather than measured effect sizes or controlled comparisons. The statements align DTx with other evidence-based MDD treatments and outline practical pathways, but they do not quantify clinical outcomes or cost-effectiveness. External validity is limited by the US/European focus and the lack of patient/public representation in the panel.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The consensus provides a pragmatic framework for clinicians to consider DTx as part of stepped-care, but adoption should still be individualized and monitored for engagement and safety until higher-quality evidence accumulates.

item.title: [14] Clinical Course and Discontinuation of Olanzapine Long-Acting Injectable: A Retrospective Case Series Including a Case of Post-Injection Delirium/Sedation Syndrome.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective case series examined real-world discontinuation rates and reasons for stopping olanzapine long-acting injectable (OLAI) in 30 outpatients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders across three behavioral health clinics, focusing on barriers such as post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome (PDSS) and monitoring burden.
FINDINGS: OLAI was discontinued in 19 patients (63.3%). Reasons included refusal/nonadherence (n=7), perceived lack of efficacy (n=5), adverse effects (n=4), transfer of care (n=3), monitoring burden (n=3), operational barriers (n=2), medication shortage (n=1), and PDSS (n=1). PDSS occurred after extended OLAI tolerability and required emergency evaluation with several days of delirium.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides descriptive real-world data but is limited by its small, retrospective, uncontrolled design and lack of standardized outcome assessment. The high discontinuation rate (63.3%) and heterogeneous reasons suggest practical and tolerability challenges, particularly the 3-hour post-injection monitoring burden. PDSS, though rare, had severe consequences. The evidence is preliminary and does not support causal inferences about risk factors or predictors of discontinuation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate high discontinuation rates with OLAI due to nonadherence, perceived inefficacy, and logistical barriers. PDSS, though uncommon, is a serious risk requiring emergency preparedness. These findings support careful patient selection, shared decision-making, and local protocol optimization rather than broad changes in practice based on risk-factor inference.

item.title: [13] Mobile Units for Integrated Addiction and HIV Prevention Services for People Who Inject Drugs: The HPTN 094 Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This open-label randomized clinical trial (HPTN 094) tested whether mobile units delivering integrated HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) with peer navigation improved PrEP and MOUD use compared with peer navigation alone in people who inject drugs (PWID) across five U.S. cities.
FINDINGS: At 26 weeks, confirmed PrEP use was 5.4% (11/203) in the intervention arm vs 2.9% (6/206) in controls (p-value not reported), and MOUD use was 14.8% (30/203) vs 10.7% (22/206). At 52 weeks, PrEP use was 2.0% (4/203) vs 1.9% (4/206) and MOUD use was 13.3% (27/203) vs 14.1% (29/206). HIV incidence was low (0.9 per 100 person-years; 95% CI 0.2–2.6), with 1 vs 2 acquisitions. All-cause mortality was lower in the intervention arm (4 vs 13 deaths; hazard ratio 0.29; 95% CI 0.1–0.9; P = .03).
INTERPRETATION: The trial shows no meaningful improvement in PrEP or MOUD uptake from mobile integrated services versus peer navigation alone, despite a mortality signal favoring the intervention. The mortality finding is intriguing but should be interpreted cautiously due to the open-label design, small event count, and lack of adjustment for multiple comparisons. The low PrEP uptake in both arms highlights persistent barriers to prevention engagement among PWID.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Mobile integrated services did not outperform peer navigation for primary outcomes, so current practice should prioritize accessible peer navigation and harm reduction services. The mortality reduction merits further investigation but is not yet sufficient to change policy or practice.

item.title: [12] One-year efficacy of the LIFESTYLE intervention in improving diet, physical activity and reducing alcohol use in overweight people with severe mental illness: multicentre randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: People with severe mental illness (SMI) have high rates of unhealthy diet, physical inactivity and alcohol use, contributing to premature mortality. This multicentre RCT from six Italian universities tested whether the structured LIFESTYLE psychoeducational programme improves diet, physical activity and reduces alcohol use versus a less structured psychoeducational comparator in 401 adults with SMI over 1 year.
FINDINGS: At 1-year follow-up, the intervention increased odds of higher weekly METs for total activity (OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.08–1.89; p<0.01), walking (OR 1.50, 95% CI 1.18–1.90; p<0.001) and moderate activity (OR 1.85, 95% CI 1.24–2.77; p<0.01). Dietary improvements included higher intake of fish (OR 1.67, 95% CI 1.45–1.97; p<0.05), fresh fruit (OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.05–1.76; p<0.05) and vegetables (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.56–1.96; p<0.05), reduced junk food (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.63–0.99; p<0.05) and lower daily alcohol use (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52–0.95; p<0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The trial shows moderate but statistically significant improvements in lifestyle metrics at 1 year, with effect sizes modest (ORs mostly 1.3–1.9). The multicentre design and use of GEE strengthen internal validity, but blinding was not possible and the comparator was an active psychoeducational programme, limiting the ability to attribute effects solely to the LIFESTYLE structure. Long-term clinical outcomes (e.g., cardiovascular events, BMI, mortality) were not assessed, so clinical significance remains uncertain. External validity may be limited to Italian SMI populations receiving structured psychoeducation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The LIFESTYLE programme may be a useful adjunct to routine care for improving diet, activity and alcohol use in SMI, but the modest effect sizes and lack of hard clinical endpoints suggest it should be implemented alongside, rather than as a replacement for, standard lifestyle interventions. Monitor adherence and sustainability of changes in real-world settings.

item.title: [11] From Toad Venom to Drug Development: The Clinical Pharmacology of Mebufotenin (5-MeO-DMT) in Treatment-Resistant Depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the clinical pharmacology of mebufotenin (5-MeO-DMT) as a potential treatment for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), summarising receptor binding, metabolism, and early clinical efficacy data from a single phase 2b trial.
FINDINGS: Mebufotenin shows high affinity for 5-HT1A (Ki 3.0 nM) and 30–300-fold lower affinity for 5-HT2A, with clearance via monoamine oxidase A. In the phase 2b trial (GH001-TRD-201), inhaled GH001 produced a placebo-adjusted MADRS reduction of −15.5 points at day 8 (p < 0.001; d = −2.0), with 57.5% (23/40) achieving remission versus 0% (0/41) on placebo. Among remitters, 87.0% (20/23) remained in remission at 6 months with as-needed retreatment. Psychoactive effects lasted 9–14 minutes, and 97.5% of patients were discharge-ready within 1 hour. No serious treatment-related adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and rests on a single small phase 2b trial without protocol-mandated psychotherapy, limiting generalisability and raising questions about expectancy effects and the role of psychological support. The large effect size (d = −2.0) and high remission rate are striking but require replication in larger, adequately blinded phase 3 trials with diverse populations to confirm efficacy, durability, and safety. The short duration of action and lack of serious adverse events are notable, but long-term risks remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data suggest potential rapid antidepressant effects of inhaled 5-MeO-DMT in TRD, but routine use cannot be recommended until robust phase 3 evidence is available. Clinicians should await larger trials before considering this intervention outside research settings.

item.title: [10] Comparative Effectiveness of Haloperidol, Droperidol, and Ondansetron for Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome in the Emergency Department.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter retrospective cohort study (2014–2024) compared haloperidol, droperidol, and ondansetron for adults with suspected cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) in the ED, focusing on short-term ED recidivism and secondary outcomes such as hospital admission and adverse events.
FINDINGS: After propensity-score matching, 72-hour ED recidivism was lower with haloperidol vs. ondansetron (8.2% vs. 15.1%; OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.41–0.62; p < 0.0001) and with droperidol vs. ondansetron (7.4% vs. 14.0%; OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32–0.76; p = 0.0014). No significant difference was found between droperidol and haloperidol (7.5% vs. 9.8%; OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47–1.20; p = 0.23).
